rail_guard.text: Brighton Station. The roof's from 1883, all iron and glass. On a summer Saturday half of London comes off these platforms with a bucket and spade.
All aboard! Trains run to everywhere you've been.

br_rock_seller.text: Brighton rock! Pink on the outside, mint on the inside, and BRIGHTON written all the way through, every slice.
The letters are made long and fat, then the whole lump is stretched and rolled till they're tiny. It's a craft. A sticky, sticky craft.

br_gull_victim.text: A gull took my chips. The whole portion. Looked me in the eye, said nothing, took the lot.
The man on the pier said it's my fault for holding them like that. How else do you hold chips?

br_volks_driver.text: All aboard for Black Rock! Magnus Volk built this in 1883: the first public electric railway in Britain, and the oldest still running anywhere.
His son reckoned the old man was always tinkering. He wired his own house up for electric light too, when most people in Brighton still had gas.

br_starling_watcher.text: Come back at dusk in winter. Thousands of starlings pour in from the downs and swirl round the West Pier like smoke, then drop into the ironwork all at once.
Nobody knows exactly how they keep from crashing. Each bird watches its seven nearest neighbours, they reckon. I can't even keep track of my own kids.

br_pride_steward.text: Pride's in August: the parade comes right down the seafront, then up to the park for the party. Everyone's welcome, and I mean everyone. Even the gulls get glitter.
My nan marched in the first one, in 1973. There were a few dozen of them. She says the rain was the same.

br_old_salt.text: Brighton was a fishing town, Brighthelmstone, long before any prince came. The boats were hauled up the shingle by capstan. A few still are.
Dr Russell from Lewes started all this, in the 1750s: drink seawater, bathe in it, he said. People came for the cure. They stayed for the pier.

then.text: Listen to that: mods and rockers revving side by side down Madeira Drive, and nobody's thrown a deckchair. Lovely.
You got the Ace Face and Terry to shake hands, and a stick of rock each to seal it. That's diplomacy, that is.
Here: a mod's target badge. The RAF roundel, nicked for a fashion statement in the sixties. Wear it and you'll be first off the line.
Beat the Ace Face, on the end of the pier, and Ton-Up Terry, down Madeira Drive. Then a peace offering from the Rock Shop in the Lanes. Everybody likes rock.

else.text: {greeting} I'm running the anniversary scooter rally. Mods AND rockers, together, down Madeira Drive. Like 1964, but without the arrests.
In 1964 the papers called it a war. It was mostly a lot of lads in a bad mood in the rain, a few broken deckchairs, and a lot of headlines.
The Ace Face won't ride with the rockers, and Ton-Up Terry won't ride with the mods. Win them round for me? They only listen to people who beat them.

then.text: Ride with the mods? ...Go on, then. But I'm at the front.
A 'ton' is a hundred miles an hour. We used to do it on the bypass, from the café to the roundabout and back before the record finished on the jukebox.
Scooters? Hairdryers on wheels. Come on, then.
Alright, I'll ride in the rally. I'll even nod at a scooter. Once.

else.text: Clear off, I'm polishing. This tank's seen more Brighton seafront than the gulls have.

then.text: We'll be there. Pressed, polished and in formation. Tell Terry to keep his oil to himself.
They call me the Ace Face. Best suit, best scooter, best dancer on the pier. Forty mirrors on my Lambretta, and I can see you in every one of them.
You want the mods at the rally? You'll have to beat the best of us first. I don't lose, mate. I've never had the time.
Fine. The mods will ride. Somebody has to show the rockers how it's done.

else.text: Mind the suit. It's mohair. It cost more than your shoes and it looks it.
